questions.question_html: A charge Q is distributed over two concentric conducting thin spherical shells radii r and R (R > r). If the surface charge densities on the two shells are equal, the electric potential at the common centre is :
questions.explanation_text: Let the charges on inner and outer spheres are Q 1 and Q 2 . $\therefore$ Q 1 + Q 2 = Q ...(1) Since charge density ' $\sigma$ ' is same for both spheres, so $\sigma$ = $\frac{Q_{1}}{4\pi r^{2}}=\frac{Q_{2}}{4\pi R^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{Q_{1}}{Q_{2}}=\frac{r^{2}}{R^{2}}$ ....(2) From (1) and (2), $\frac{Q_{2}r^{2}}{R^{2}}+Q_{2}=Q$ $\Rightarrow$ Q 2 = $\frac{QR^{2}}{(r^{2}+R^{2})}$ $\therefore$ Q 1 = $\frac{r^{2}}{R^{2}}.\frac{QR^{2}}{(r^{2}+R^{2})}$ = $\frac{Qr^{2}}{(r^{2}+R^{2})}$ Potential at centre 'O' = $\frac{kQ_{1}}{r}+\frac{kQ_{2}}{R}$ = $k[\frac{Qr^{2}}{r(r^{2}+R^{2})}+\frac{QR^{2}}{R(r^{2}+R^{2})}]$ = $\frac{kQ(r+R)}{(r^{2}+R^{2})}$ = $\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}}\frac{(R+r)}{(R^{2}+r^{2})}$ Q
questions.explanation_html:
Let the charges on inner and outer spheres are Q1 and Q2.

$\therefore$ Q1 + Q2 = Q ...(1)

Since charge density ' $\sigma$ ' is same for both spheres, so

$\sigma$ = $\frac{Q_{1}}{4\pi r^{2}}=\frac{Q_{2}}{4\pi R^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{Q_{1}}{Q_{2}}=\frac{r^{2}}{R^{2}}$ ....(2)

From (1) and (2),

$\frac{Q_{2}r^{2}}{R^{2}}+Q_{2}=Q$

$\Rightarrow$ Q2 = $\frac{QR^{2}}{(r^{2}+R^{2})}$

$\therefore$ Q1 = $\frac{r^{2}}{R^{2}}.\frac{QR^{2}}{(r^{2}+R^{2})}$ = $\frac{Qr^{2}}{(r^{2}+R^{2})}$

Potential at centre 'O' = $\frac{kQ_{1}}{r}+\frac{kQ_{2}}{R}$

= $k[\frac{Qr^{2}}{r(r^{2}+R^{2})}+\frac{QR^{2}}{R(r^{2}+R^{2})}]$

= $\frac{kQ(r+R)}{(r^{2}+R^{2})}$

= $\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}}\frac{(R+r)}{(R^{2}+r^{2})}$ Q

questions.explanation_text: Applying mechanical energy conservation, $K_{A}+U_{A}=K_{B}+U_{B}$ $\Rightarrow$ $0+mgy+qV_{A}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+0+(+qV_{B})$ $\Rightarrow$ $mgy+qV_{A}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+q(V_{B})$ $\Rightarrow$ $mgy+\frac{qk(Q)}{R}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+\frac{qk(Q)}{R+y}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}=-\frac{kq(Q)}{R+y}+\frac{kq(Q)}{R}+mgy$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{mv^{2}}{2}=\frac{-kq(Q)R+kq(Q)(R+y)}{R(R+y)}+mgy$ $\Rightarrow$ $v^{2}=\frac{2}{m}[\frac{-kqQR+kqQR+kqQ}{R(R+y)}+mgy]$ $\Rightarrow$ $v^{2}=\frac{2}{m}[\frac{kq(Q)y}{R(R+y)}+mgy]$ $\Rightarrow$ $v^{2}=2y[\frac{q(Q)}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}R(R+y)m}+g]=2y[\frac{qQ}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}R(R+y)m}+g]$
questions.explanation_html:
Applying mechanical energy conservation,

$K_{A}+U_{A}=K_{B}+U_{B}$

$\Rightarrow$ $0+mgy+qV_{A}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+0+(+qV_{B})$

$\Rightarrow$ $mgy+qV_{A}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+q(V_{B})$

$\Rightarrow$ $mgy+\frac{qk(Q)}{R}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+\frac{qk(Q)}{R+y}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}=-\frac{kq(Q)}{R+y}+\frac{kq(Q)}{R}+mgy$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{mv^{2}}{2}=\frac{-kq(Q)R+kq(Q)(R+y)}{R(R+y)}+mgy$

$\Rightarrow$ $v^{2}=\frac{2}{m}[\frac{-kqQR+kqQR+kqQ}{R(R+y)}+mgy]$

$\Rightarrow$ $v^{2}=\frac{2}{m}[\frac{kq(Q)y}{R(R+y)}+mgy]$

$\Rightarrow$ $v^{2}=2y[\frac{q(Q)}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}R(R+y)m}+g]=2y[\frac{qQ}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}R(R+y)m}+g]$

questions.explanation_text: Let particle have charge q and mass 'm We know, F = ma y = qE $\therefore$ $a_{y}=\frac{qE}{m}$ As electric field is along vertical direction so horizontal component of acceleration is zero. $\therefore$ a x = 0 Applying, $S=u_{y}t+\frac{1}{2}a_{y}t^{2}$ $-y=0 \times t+\frac{1}{2}(\frac{qE}{m})t^{2}$ ....(1) Also, $x=V_{0}t$ $\Rightarrow t=\frac{x}{V_{0}}$ Putting in (1) we get, $y=-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{qE}{m})(\frac{x}{V_{0}})^{2}$ Differentiating with respect to x, $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{qE}{m}(\frac{x}{V_{0}^{2}})$ $\therefore$ Slope = $m=tan\theta=-\frac{qE}{m}(\frac{x}{V_{0}^{2}})$ when x = d, then $m=-\frac{qE}{m}(\frac{d}{V_{0}^{2}})$ We know, equation of straight line whose slope is m, y = mx + c Here m = $(-\frac{qEd}{mV_{0}^{2}})$ , $\therefore$ $-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{qE}{m})(\frac{d}{V_{0}})^{2}=(-\frac{qEd}{mV_{0}^{2}})d+c$ $\Rightarrow$ c = $\frac{qEd}{2mV_{0}^{2}}$ Putting the value of c, we get $y=-(\frac{qEd}{mV_{0}^{2}})x+\frac{qEd^{2}}{2mV_{0}^{2}}$ $=\frac{qEd}{mV_{0}^{2}}(\frac{d}{2}-x)$
questions.explanation_html:
Let particle have charge q and mass 'm

We know, F = may = qE

$\therefore$ $a_{y}=\frac{qE}{m}$

As electric field is along vertical direction so horizontal component of acceleration is zero.

$\therefore$ ax = 0

Applying, $S=u_{y}t+\frac{1}{2}a_{y}t^{2}$

$-y=0 \times t+\frac{1}{2}(\frac{qE}{m})t^{2}$ ....(1)

Also, $x=V_{0}t$

$\Rightarrow t=\frac{x}{V_{0}}$

Putting in (1) we get,

$y=-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{qE}{m})(\frac{x}{V_{0}})^{2}$

Differentiating with respect to x,

$\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{qE}{m}(\frac{x}{V_{0}^{2}})$

$\therefore$ Slope = $m=tan\theta=-\frac{qE}{m}(\frac{x}{V_{0}^{2}})$

when x = d, then $m=-\frac{qE}{m}(\frac{d}{V_{0}^{2}})$

We know, equation of straight line whose slope is m,

y = mx + c

Here m = $(-\frac{qEd}{mV_{0}^{2}})$ ,

$\therefore$ $-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{qE}{m})(\frac{d}{V_{0}})^{2}=(-\frac{qEd}{mV_{0}^{2}})d+c$

$\Rightarrow$ c = $\frac{qEd}{2mV_{0}^{2}}$

Putting the value of c, we get

$y=-(\frac{qEd}{mV_{0}^{2}})x+\frac{qEd^{2}}{2mV_{0}^{2}}$

$=\frac{qEd}{mV_{0}^{2}}(\frac{d}{2}-x)$

questions.question_text:
A solid conducting sphere, having a charge Q,
is surrounded by an uncharged conducting
hollow spherical shell. Let the potential
difference between the surface of the solid
sphere and that of the outer surface of the
hollow shell be V. If the shell is now given a
charge of –4 Q, the new potential difference
between the same two surfaces is :
questions.question_html: A solid conducting sphere, having a charge Q, is surrounded by an uncharged conducting hollow spherical shell. Let the potential difference between the surface of the solid sphere and that of the outer surface of the hollow shell be V. If the shell is now given a charge of –4 Q, the new potential difference between the same two surfaces is :
questions.explanation_text: Initially when uncharged shell encloses charge Q, charge distribution due to induction will be as shown, The potential on surface of inner shell is $V_{A}=\frac{kQ}{a}+\frac{k(-Q)}{b}+\frac{kQ}{b}$ ..... (i) where, k = proportionality constant. Potential on surface of outer shell is $V_{B}=\frac{kQ}{b}+\frac{k(-Q)}{b}+\frac{kQ}{b}$ ..... (ii) Then, potential difference is $\Delta V_{AB}=V_{A}-V_{B}=kQ(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b})$ Given, $\Delta V_{AB}=V$ So, $kQ(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b})=V$ ....... (iii) Finally after giving charge $-$ 4Q to outer shell, potential difference will be $\Delta V_{AB}=V_{A}-V_{B}$ $=(\frac{kQ}{a}+\frac{k(-4Q)}{b})-(\frac{kQ}{b}+\frac{k(-4Q)}{b})$ $=kQ(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b})=V$ [from Eq. (iii)] Hence, we obtain that potential difference does not depend on the charge of outer sphere, hence potential difference remains same.
questions.explanation_html:
Initially when uncharged shell encloses charge Q, charge distribution due to induction will be as shown,

The potential on surface of inner shell is

$V_{A}=\frac{kQ}{a}+\frac{k(-Q)}{b}+\frac{kQ}{b}$ ..... (i)

where, k = proportionality constant.

Potential on surface of outer shell is

$V_{B}=\frac{kQ}{b}+\frac{k(-Q)}{b}+\frac{kQ}{b}$ ..... (ii)

Then, potential difference is

$\Delta V_{AB}=V_{A}-V_{B}=kQ(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b})$

Given, $\Delta V_{AB}=V$

So, $kQ(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b})=V$ ....... (iii)

Finally after giving charge $-$ 4Q to outer shell, potential difference will be

$\Delta V_{AB}=V_{A}-V_{B}$

$=(\frac{kQ}{a}+\frac{k(-4Q)}{b})-(\frac{kQ}{b}+\frac{k(-4Q)}{b})$

$=kQ(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{b})=V$ [from Eq. (iii)]

Hence, we obtain that potential difference does not depend on the charge of outer sphere, hence potential difference remains same.

questions.explanation_html:
Volume of this spherical layer,

dv = (4 $\pi$ r2)dr

charge present in this layer,

dq = $\rho$ (4 $\pi$ r2 dr)

= $\frac{A}{r^{2}}e^{-\frac{2r}{a}}(4\pi r^{2}dr)$

= $Ae^{-\frac{2r}{a}}(4\pi dr)$

$\therefore$   Total charge in the sphere,

Q= $\int_{0}^{R}4\pi Ae^{-\frac{2r}{a}}dr$

= 4 $\pi$ A $\int_{0}^{R}e^{-\frac{2r}{a}}dr$

= 4 $\pi$ A $[\frac{e^{-\frac{2r}{a}}}{-\frac{2}{a}}]_{0}^{R}$

= 4 $\pi$ A $(-\frac{a}{2})(e^{-\frac{2R}{a}}-1)$

$\therefore$   Q = 2 $\pi$ aA $(1-e^{-\frac{2R}{a}})$

$\Rightarrow$    $1-e^{-\frac{2R}{a}}$ = $\frac{Q}{2\pi aA}$

$\Rightarrow$    $e^{-\frac{2R}{a}}$ = 1 $-$ $\frac{Q}{2\pi aA}$

$\Rightarrow$    $e^{\frac{2R}{a}}$ = $\frac{1}{1-\frac{Q}{2\pi aA}}$

$\Rightarrow$    $\frac{2R}{a}=log(\frac{1}{1-\frac{Q}{2\pi aA}})$

$\Rightarrow$   R = $\frac{a}{2}$ log $(\frac{1}{1-\frac{Q}{2\pi aA}})$

questions.question_text: Two point charges q 1 $(\sqrt{10}\mu C)$ and q 2 ( $-$ 25 $\mu$ C) are placed on the x-axis at x = 1 m and x = 4 m respectively. The electric field (in V/m) at a point y = 3 m on y-axis is, [take $\frac{1}{4\pi\in_{0}}$ = 9 $\times$ 10 9 Nm 2 C $-$ 2 ]
questions.question_html:
Two point charges q1 $(\sqrt{10}\mu C)$ and q2( $-$ 25 $\mu$ C) are placed on the x-axis at x = 1 m and x = 4 m respectively. The electric field (in V/m) at a point y = 3 m on y-axis is,
[take $\frac{1}{4\pi\in_{0}}$ = 9 $\times$ 109 Nm2C $-$ 2]
questions.explanation_text: Electric field due to $\sqrt{10}\mu C$ charge : $\vec{E_{1}}=-$ E 1 sin $\theta$ 1 $\hat{i}$ + E 1 cos $\theta$ 1 $\hat{j}$ Where, E 1 $=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}} \times \frac{|q_{1}|}{r_{1}^{2}}$ $=9 \times 10^{9} \times \frac{\sqrt{10} \times 10^{-6}}{(\sqrt{1^{2}}+3^{2})^{2}}$ $=\frac{9 \times 10^{3}}{\sqrt{10}}v/m$ sin $\theta$ 1 $=$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$ and cos $\theta$ 1 = $\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{E_{1}}=\frac{9 \times 10^{3}}{\sqrt{10}}(-\frac{1}{10}\hat{i}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\hat{j})$ $=9 \times 10^{2}(-\hat{i}+3\hat{j})$ Electric field due to $-$ 25 $\mu$ C charge, $\vec{E_{2}}=$ E 2 sin $\theta$ 2 $\hat{i}$ $-$ E 2 cos $\theta$ 2 $\hat{j}$ where E 2 $=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}} \times \frac{|9_{2}|}{r_{2}^{2}}$ $=9 \times 10^{9} \times \frac{25 \times 10^{-6}}{(\sqrt{4^{2}+3^{2}})^{2}}$ $=9 \times 10^{3}$ V/m sin $\theta$ 2 = $\frac{4}{5}$ and cos $\theta$ 2 = $\frac{3}{5}$ $\therefore$ $\vec{E_{2}}=9 \times 10^{3}(\frac{4}{5}\hat{i}-\frac{3}{5}\hat{j})$ $=18 \times 10^{2}(4\hat{i}-3\hat{j})$ $\therefore$ Net electric field, $\vec{E}$ = $\vec{E}_{1}$ + $\vec{E}_{2}$ $=(63\hat{i}-27\hat{j}) \times 10^{2}V/m$
questions.explanation_html:
Electric field due to $\sqrt{10}\mu C$ charge :

$\vec{E_{1}}=-$ E1 sin $\theta$ 1 $\hat{i}$ + E1 cos $\theta$ 1 $\hat{j}$

Where,

E1 $=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}} \times \frac{|q_{1}|}{r_{1}^{2}}$

$=9 \times 10^{9} \times \frac{\sqrt{10} \times 10^{-6}}{(\sqrt{1^{2}}+3^{2})^{2}}$

$=\frac{9 \times 10^{3}}{\sqrt{10}}v/m$

sin $\theta$ 1 $=$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$

and cos $\theta$ 1 = $\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}$

$\therefore$     $\vec{E_{1}}=\frac{9 \times 10^{3}}{\sqrt{10}}(-\frac{1}{10}\hat{i}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\hat{j})$

$=9 \times 10^{2}(-\hat{i}+3\hat{j})$

Electric field due to $-$ 25 $\mu$ C charge,



$\vec{E_{2}}=$ E2 sin $\theta$ 2 $\hat{i}$ $-$ E2 cos $\theta$ 2 $\hat{j}$

where

E2 $=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}} \times \frac{|9_{2}|}{r_{2}^{2}}$

$=9 \times 10^{9} \times \frac{25 \times 10^{-6}}{(\sqrt{4^{2}+3^{2}})^{2}}$

$=9 \times 10^{3}$ V/m

sin $\theta$ 2 = $\frac{4}{5}$

and cos $\theta$ 2 = $\frac{3}{5}$

$\therefore$     $\vec{E_{2}}=9 \times 10^{3}(\frac{4}{5}\hat{i}-\frac{3}{5}\hat{j})$

$=18 \times 10^{2}(4\hat{i}-3\hat{j})$

$\therefore$    Net electric field,

$\vec{E}$ = $\vec{E}_{1}$ + $\vec{E}_{2}$

$=(63\hat{i}-27\hat{j}) \times 10^{2}V/m$

An electric dipole has a fixed dipole moment $\vec{p}$ , which makes angle $\theta$ with respect to x-axis. When

questions.question_html: An electric dipole has a fixed dipole moment $\vec{p}$ , which makes angle $\theta$ with respect to x-axis. When subjected to an electric field $\vec{E_{1}}=E\hat{i}$ , it experiences a torque $\vec{T_{1}}=\tau\hat{k}$ . When subjected to another electric field $\vec{E_{2}}=\sqrt{3}E_{1}\hat{j}$ it experiences a torque $\vec{T_{2}}=\vec{-T_{1}}$ . The angle $\theta$ is:
questions.explanation_text:
Torque experienced by the dipole in an
electric field, $T$ = pE sin $\theta$ $\vec{T}=\vec{p} \times \vec{E}$ $\vec{p}=pcos\theta\hat{i}+psin\theta\hat{j}$ $\vec{E_{1}}=E\hat{i}$ $\vec{T_{1}}=\vec{P} \times \vec{E}_{1}$ = ( $pcos\theta\hat{i}+psin\theta\hat{j}$ ) $\times$ $E(\hat{i})$ = pE sin $\theta$ $(-\hat{k})$ $\vec{E_{2}}=\sqrt{3}E_{1}\hat{j}$ $\vec{T_{2}}=$ ( $pcos\theta\hat{i}+psin\theta\hat{j}$ ) $\times$ $\sqrt{3}E_{1}\hat{j}$ = $\sqrt{3}pEcos\theta(\hat{k})$ Now given, $\vec{T_{2}}$ = $-\vec{T_{1}}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\sqrt{3}pEcos\theta(\hat{k})$ = -pE sin $\theta$ $(-\hat{k})$ $\Rightarrow$ $tan\theta=\sqrt{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\theta$ = 60 o
questions.explanation_html:
Torque experienced by the dipole in an electric field,

$T$ = pE sin $\theta$

$\vec{T}=\vec{p} \times \vec{E}$

$\vec{p}=pcos\theta\hat{i}+psin\theta\hat{j}$

$\vec{E_{1}}=E\hat{i}$

$\vec{T_{1}}=\vec{P} \times \vec{E}_{1}$

= ( $pcos\theta\hat{i}+psin\theta\hat{j}$ ) $\times$ $E(\hat{i})$

= pE sin $\theta$ $(-\hat{k})$

$\vec{E_{2}}=\sqrt{3}E_{1}\hat{j}$

$\vec{T_{2}}=$ ( $pcos\theta\hat{i}+psin\theta\hat{j}$ ) $\times$ $\sqrt{3}E_{1}\hat{j}$

= $\sqrt{3}pEcos\theta(\hat{k})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\sqrt{3}pEcos\theta(\hat{k})$ = -pE sin $\theta$ $(-\hat{k})$

$\Rightarrow$ $tan\theta=\sqrt{3}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\theta$ = 60o

$F_{B}^{'}=V(d-\rho)g=V(1.6-0.8)g=0.8Vg$
$=0.8\frac{m}{d}g=\frac{0.8mg}{1.6}=\frac{mg}{2}$
$\therefore$ $mg=\frac{mg}{2}+T^{'}cos15^{\circ}$
$\Rightarrow \frac{mg}{2}=T^{'}cos15^{\circ}$ $...(B)$
From $(A)$ and $(B),$ $tan15^{\circ}=\frac{2F_{e}^{'}}{mg}...(2)$
From $(1)$ and $(2)$
$\frac{F_{e}}{mg}=\frac{2F_{e}^{'}}{mg} \Rightarrow F_{e}=2F_{e}^{'} \Rightarrow F_{e}^{'}=\frac{F_{e}}{2}$

questions.explanation_text: Let us consider a spherical shell of radius $x$ and thickness $dx.$ Charge on this shell $dq=\rho.4\pi^{2}dx=\rho_{0}(\frac{5}{4}-\frac{x}{R}).4\pi x^{2}dx$ $\therefore$ Total charge in the spherical region from center to $r$ $(r<R)$ is $q=\int dq=4\pi\rho_{0}\int_{0}^{r}(\frac{5}{4}-\frac{x}{R})x^{2}dx$ $=4\pi\rho_{0}[\frac{5}{4}.\frac{r^{3}}{3}-\frac{1}{R}.\frac{r^{4}}{4}]$ $=\pi\rho_{0}r^{3}(\frac{5}{3}-\frac{r}{R})$ $\therefore$ Electric field at $r,$ $E=\frac{1}{4\pi\in_{0}}.\frac{q}{r^{2}}$ $=\frac{1}{4\pi\in_{0}}.\frac{\pi\rho_{0}r^{3}}{r^{2}}(\frac{5}{3}-\frac{r}{R})$ $=\frac{\rho_{0}r}{4\in_{0}}(\frac{5}{3}-\frac{r}{R})$
questions.explanation_html:
Let us consider a spherical shell of radius $x$ and thickness $dx.$

Charge on this shell

$dq=\rho.4\pi^{2}dx=\rho_{0}(\frac{5}{4}-\frac{x}{R}).4\pi x^{2}dx$

$\therefore$ Total charge in the spherical region from center to $r$ $(r<R)$ is

$q=\int dq=4\pi\rho_{0}\int_{0}^{r}(\frac{5}{4}-\frac{x}{R})x^{2}dx$

$=4\pi\rho_{0}[\frac{5}{4}.\frac{r^{3}}{3}-\frac{1}{R}.\frac{r^{4}}{4}]$

$=\pi\rho_{0}r^{3}(\frac{5}{3}-\frac{r}{R})$

$\therefore$ Electric field at $r,$ $E=\frac{1}{4\pi\in_{0}}.\frac{q}{r^{2}}$

$=\frac{1}{4\pi\in_{0}}.\frac{\pi\rho_{0}r^{3}}{r^{2}}(\frac{5}{3}-\frac{r}{R})$

$=\frac{\rho_{0}r}{4\in_{0}}(\frac{5}{3}-\frac{r}{R})$
